Saying 'gainful job' in very formal writing where 'gainful employment' is standard.

senses.definition: In the Bible, the eldest son of Moses, and also a son of Levi, founder of a Levite clan, both named for the Hebrew phrase meaning 'a stranger there'.

core.definition: In the Bible, the eldest son of Moses, and also a son of Levi, founder of a Levite clan, both named for the Hebrew phrase meaning 'a stranger there'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'sh' is a single sound, as in 'shoe'. The final syllable is a weak 'um', not a full 'ahm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper name used in religious study and Bible discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter Gershom mainly in Bible study, church teaching and seminary contexts. It is a personal name too, though less common. When discussing the Bible, people usually say 'Moses' son Gershom' to make clear which person is meant.

distinctions.note: Gershon is the spelling used for Levi's son in Genesis and Numbers, while Gershom is used for Moses' son in Exodus. Both names are close in form, so check the context.

examples.everyday: At Bible study last night, someone asked who Gershom was, and I said he was Moses' oldest son.
examples.professional: In my sermon series on Exodus, I mentioned Gershom to show how Moses described his life as a foreigner.
examples.analytical: The name Gershom in Exodus 2:22 reflects Moses' own experience of exile, and the wordplay on 'stranger' shapes the narrative's meaning.

nuance.analogy: Gershom is like a family surname that marks a person's place as an outsider, carrying the story of where his father had been.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Gershom, from ger, 'stranger, sojourner', plus sham, 'there'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'sh' as a 'ch' or 's' sound.
Confusing Gershom with Gershon, who is Levi's son in Genesis and Numbers.
nuance.biblical_note: Gershom is the Hebrew name Gershom, meaning 'stranger there' (ger, 'stranger', plus sham, 'there'). Exodus 2:22 says Moses named his son Gershom, explaining that he had become a sojourner in a foreign land. Exodus 18:3 repeats this, when Moses' father-in-law Jethro brings Gershom and Moses' wife Zipporah back to him. 1 Chronicles 23:15 lists Gershom among the sons of Levi, linking the name to the Levitical line.

senses.definition: To avoid or bypass an obstacle.
senses.example: Tax consultants look for ways to get around the law.

senses.definition: To move to the other side of (something, such as an obstruction) by deviating from a direct course or following a curved path.
senses.example: The tide was too high, and we couldn't get around the rocks.

senses.definition: To transport oneself from place to place.
senses.example: How's he gonna get around without a car?

senses.definition: To visit numerous different places.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see get,‎ around.
To circumvent the obligation and performance of a chore; to get out of.
senses.example: How did you get around having to write the executive report?

senses.definition: To be sexually promiscuous.
senses.example: Wow, she really gets around.

core.definition: To travel from place to place, especially within a city or area.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'ownd'. The 'er' in 'around' is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so keep it light. Do not pronounce 'around' with a strong first vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes practical movement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use get around for moving from place to place, especially for people without a car or new to a city: 'How do you get around without a car?' It is casual. It can also mean avoiding a rule or news spreading. A natural reply is 'The bus works fine.'

distinctions.note: Travel is a general word for trips, often long ones, while get around is practical and usually about moving within a local area.
Get by means to manage with limited resources, not to move from place to place.

examples.everyday: We get around town mostly on the subway, so we rarely need a car.
examples.professional: Our field engineers get around the plant on electric carts during inspections.
examples.analytical: Her essay argues that in a city with weak transit, the poor get around only at great cost in time and money.

nuance.analogy: Like water finding a path around a rock, you get around an obstacle by moving along a different route.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'get around' (move) with 'get around to' (finally do something), which needs 'to' plus a verb.
Pronouncing 'around' with a long first vowel instead of 'uh-ROWND'.

conversation.text: It's easy to get around Chicago without a car.
There's no way to get around the security check.
I finally got around to fixing the leaky faucet.
News gets around fast in a small town.
What's the best way to get around the city without a car?
I get around on my bike most days.
There's no way to get around the rules on this one.
I never got around to renewing my license.

senses.definition: A bitmap image in a particular format with support for multiple images per file or animations, and up to 256 distinct colors per frame, including a fully transparent color.
senses.example: I'll send you a GIF of the proposed logo.

senses.definition: Any short video without audio, usually one which loops.
Any short video, in a format directly supported by HTML5 (ie. GIF, MP4, WebM)
Abbreviation of granular iron(stone) formation.
To create a GIF file of; to create a similar animated image file of.
senses.example: He GIFed the highlights of the debate

core.definition: A compressed image format that supports short animations; also, a short looping animated clip. As a verb, to make a GIF of something.

pronunciation.tip: The word is one syllable with a short i, like "gift" without the t. The creator said it was pronounced "JIF", but the hard G is now common in the US, so either is accepted.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use GIF constantly in texting, social media and workplace chat, often for reactions, jokes or quick demonstrations. In professional settings, say "animated GIF" or "short video clip" if you want to be formal. Someone might say "Send a GIF" or "Drop a GIF in the channel" in casual chat.

distinctions.note: An MP4 is a video format with sound and higher quality; a GIF usually has no sound and uses fewer colors.
A PNG is a still image format; a GIF can contain several frames and animate.

examples.everyday: My sister sent me a funny GIF of a cat falling off a couch.
examples.professional: Could you drop a quick GIF of the bug in the team channel so we can see what happens?
examples.analytical: The GIF format's limited palette and lossless frame encoding shape the kind of motion it can represent well.

nuance.analogy: Like a flipbook made of a few dozen pictures that loops forever.
nuance.etymology: Short for Graphics Interchange Format, the format introduced by CompuServe in 1987.
common_mistakes: Using GIF as a plural in the wrong place; say "GIFs" with an s.
Saying "gif" with a soft g as in "giant" in technical discussions, where the word is usually pronounced with a hard g.

conversation.text: He replied with a funny GIF of a dancing cat.
Send me that GIF; I love it.
Our group chat is basically just GIFs.

senses.definition: An excess, too much.
senses.example: a glut of the market

senses.definition: That which is swallowed.
Something that fills up an opening.
A wooden wedge used in splitting blocks.
A piece of wood used to fill up behind cribbing or tubbing.
A bat, or small piece of brick, used to fill out a course.
(Can we verify this sense?) A block used for a fulcrum.
The broad-nosed eel (Anguilla anguilla, syn. Anguilla latirostris), found in Europe, Asia, the West Indies, etc.
An arched opening to the ashpit of a kiln.
To fill to capacity; to satisfy all demand or requirement; to sate.
senses.example: to glut one's appetite

senses.definition: To provide (a market) with so much of a product that the supply greatly exceeds the demand.
To eat gluttonously or to satiety.

core.definition: An excess or oversupply of something, so that there is far more than is needed or wanted.

pronunciation.tip: It has one syllable with a short 'uh' vowel, like 'cut' and 'but.' Do not stretch the vowel into 'glaht' or 'gloot.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It implies too much of something, which can be wasteful, unhealthy, or bad for prices.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glut in business and news, as in 'a glut of housing' or 'a glut on the market.' In everyday talk people often say 'too much' or 'more than enough,' but glut sounds natural in economic discussions. Using it for food sounds more informal and slightly dramatic.

distinctions.note: Surplus is a neutral term for extra supply; glut suggests a larger, more problematic excess that pushes prices down.
Excess is a general word for too much; glut is more specific to supply, markets, or overabundance.

examples.everyday: There's a glut of zucchini in our garden this year, so I keep giving it away.
examples.professional: We have a glut of unused licenses, so finance wants us to cut the subscription before renewal.
examples.analytical: Economists argue that a glut of savings can depress interest rates even when investment opportunities are limited.

nuance.analogy: Like a river overflowing its banks: there is more water than the channel can carry, so it spreads everywhere.
nuance.etymology: From Old French gloutir, to swallow, from Latin glutire.
common_mistakes: Using glut as a verb with the wrong preposition, such as glut with instead of glut the market
Confusing glut with gluttony, which describes excessive eating as a vice

glut.etymology: Middle English *glotien//glotten*, probably Old French *gloter//glotir//glotoiier* [compare, ], Latin *gluttiō*.

senses.definition: The third book of the New Testament, a Gospel traditionally ascribed to Luke, known for its emphasis on mercy, the poor and prayer.

core.definition: The third book of the New Testament, a Gospel traditionally ascribed to Luke, known for its emphasis on mercy, the poor and prayer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GAH and LOOK, and 'of' reduces to 'uv'. Luke rhymes with 'book', so the vowel is short, not the long 'oo' of 'loose'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a reference; reverent in religious use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the Gospel of Luke' in formal settings and just 'Luke' in Bible study, as in 'We're in Luke this month.' Pastors often mention its birth stories and parables. The capital G marks the book, while lowercase gospel means the good news.

distinctions.note: Acts was written by the same author as Luke's Gospel and continues the story into the early church.
John has a distinct theology and structure; Luke is more narrative and historical in tone.
Mark is brief and fast-paced, while Luke adds birth narratives and a formal preface.

collocations: the nativity story in the Gospel of Luke
the parables in the Gospel of Luke
the preface to the Gospel of Luke
a passage from the Gospel of Luke

examples.everyday: My daughter is memorizing the Christmas story from the Gospel of Luke for the church pageant.
examples.professional: For the workshop on mercy, I'm using the parables in the Gospel of Luke because they give the clearest examples.
examples.analytical: The preface to the Gospel of Luke claims a careful investigation of earlier accounts, and scholars read that claim as a key to its method.

nuance.analogy: Like a careful historian who interviews witnesses and arranges the story in order, Luke presents Jesus's life as a sequenced account.
nuance.etymology: From Old English godspel, 'good news,' a translation of Greek euangelion.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing Luke with a long 'oo' like 'loose'; it rhymes with 'book'.
Writing 'Gospel of Saint Luke' in everyday speech; Americans usually say 'the Gospel of Luke' or just 'Luke'.
Assuming Luke was an eyewitness to Jesus; the text does not claim that, and tradition names him as a companion of Paul.
nuance.biblical_note: Luke 1:1-4 is the author's preface to Theophilus, explaining that he has investigated the sources carefully. Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus read from Isaiah in the synagogue, announcing good news to the poor. Luke 15 contains the parables of the lost sheep, the lost coin and the prodigal son, all about God's search for the lost. The root word is Greek euangelion, 'good news.'

senses.definition: Someone who likes to talk about other people's private or personal business.
senses.example: Be careful what you say to him: he’s a bit of a gossip.

senses.definition: Idle talk about someone’s private or personal matters, especially about someone not present.
senses.example: According to the latest gossip, their relationship is on the rocks.

senses.definition: A genre in contemporary media, usually focused on the personal affairs of celebrities.
senses.example: a gossip columnist

senses.definition: Communication done using a gossip protocol.
Idle conversation in general.
Title used with the name of one's child's godparent or of a friend.
A sponsor; a godfather or godmother; the godparent of one's child or godchild, or the parent of one's godchild.
To talk about someone else's private or personal business, especially in a manner that spreads the information.
To talk idly.
To communicate using a gossip protocol.

core.definition: Idle talk about other people's private or personal affairs, often unkind or spread without their knowledge.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a short, quick 'sip' with a reduced vowel. Do not stretch the 'o' into a long 'oh' sound.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gossip' for talk about other people's private lives, usually among friends, coworkers or neighbors. It is informal, and calling someone a gossip is an insult. Informal speakers often say 'Did you hear the latest dish?' or 'Spill the tea', but 'gossip' is the neutral word. A natural reply to a juicy story is 'No way! Tell me more.'

distinctions.note: A rumor is an unverified claim spread about a situation, while gossip is focused on personal details about a particular person.
A chat is a friendly conversation about anything, while gossip specifically involves talking about others' private matters.

examples.everyday: Don't tell Maria that, she loves to spread gossip about the neighbors.
examples.professional: Management reminded the team that office gossip about performance reviews undermines trust.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have argued that gossip plays a social role by enforcing shared norms, although it can also cause harm.

nuance.analogy: Gossip is like a rumor mill that turns private details into a story passed hand to hand.
nuance.etymology: From Old English godsibb, meaning 'godparent', which later came to mean a close friend and then a chatty person.
common_mistakes: Using 'gossip' as a countable noun without an article, as in 'He told me a gossip' instead of 'He told me some gossip'.
Confusing 'gossip' with 'rumor' and using them interchangeably in formal writing.

gossip.etymology: From Middle English *gossib*, *godsib* (“a close friend or relation, a confidant; a godparent”), from Old English *godsibb* (“godparent, sponsor”), equivalent to *god-* + *sib*.

conversation.text: Did you hear the latest gossip about the new manager?
My aunts love to gossip at family dinners.
Don't tell Jake anything. He's such a gossip.

senses.definition: The belief that some phenomenon occurs gradually over a long period of time.
The belief that change ought to be brought about in small, discrete increments rather than in abrupt strokes such as revolutions or uprisings.
The belief that evolution proceeds at a steady pace, without the sudden development of new species or biological features from one generation to the next.

core.definition: The belief that change, whether in society, nature, or science, happens slowly through small steps rather than through sudden, dramatic events.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on GRAD, and -ism is an unstressed ending ending in a schwa. Many learners pronounce the middle syllable as 'way' rather than a reduced 'wuh'.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive in reform and science contexts, and negative when critics use it to suggest excessive delay.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'gradualism' mainly in political, historical, scientific, and academic discussion, not in casual conversation. In debates, it can be a compliment for careful reform or a criticism of moving too slowly. Use 'gradualist' for a person who holds this view.

distinctions.note: Gradualism stresses a slow, continuous process, while incrementalism in policy stresses small, tested steps that can be adjusted as results come in.
Catastrophism holds that sudden events drive major change, the opposite view from gradualism in geology and biology.

examples.everyday: He believes in gradualism, so he cut his coffee intake by one cup a week instead of quitting overnight.
examples.professional: The team's gradualism on the rewrite meant we kept the old system running for six months while we migrated users.
examples.analytical: Lyell's gradualism held that the earth's features are shaped by slow, continuous processes still observable today, rather than by sudden catastrophes.

nuance.analogy: Gradualism is like erosion: small, steady forces reshape the landscape over long periods.
nuance.etymology: From gradual and the suffix -ism, from Latin gradus, step.
common_mistakes: Confusing gradualism, the belief, with gradualist, the person who holds it.
Using gradualism for the simple fact of slowness; it means a belief or theory about change.

senses.definition: Having a lot of body hair.
senses.example: a hairy man

senses.definition: Having a lot of fur.
senses.example: hairy mammoth

senses.definition: Having hair growing from it.
senses.example: hairy chest; hairy back

senses.definition: Seeming as if hair-covered or as if consisting of hair.
senses.example: hairy cell leukemia

senses.definition: Difficult, complex, intricate, or intimidating.
senses.example: It’s a hairy problem, and will probably take several weeks to sort out.

senses.definition: Causing anxiety or fright; terrifying, scary.
Long-haired.
senses.example: yelling about dirty, hairy hippies

core.definition: Covered with a lot of hair or fur.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables, stress on the first, with the 'air' vowel and a rhotic R. Do not say 'HAY-ree'; the final y is a short ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing animals or people; informal slang for 'scary' or 'dangerous' ('a hairy situation'), which is often humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'a hairy dog' or 'a hairy chest' in neutral description, and in casual speech 'hairy' can mean a risky or messy situation. Calling a person hairy about their body can sound rude, so use it with care. The slang sense is common among friends.

distinctions.note: Furry suggests soft, thick fur on an animal or toy, while hairy is broader and can describe human body hair.
Shaggy means having long, untidy hair or fur, often with a messy look; hairy is more neutral.

examples.everyday: Our new puppy is so hairy that we vacuum the couch every day.
examples.professional: The hairy-looking lab sample turned out to be a fiber from the carpet, not a biological contaminant.
examples.analytical: In Genesis, Esau's hairy body is part of the story that lets Jacob deceive their father Isaac.

nuance.analogy: Like a sweater made of thick wool that covers everything, hairy describes a body or surface completely covered in hair.
nuance.etymology: From 'hair' (Old English hær) with the suffix '-y' meaning 'full of' or 'covered with'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hairy' with two syllables in the wrong place, as 'HAIR-ee' is correct.
Using 'hairy' as an insult about a person's body in polite company.
nuance.biblical_note: Genesis 27:11 has Jacob's mother Rebekah point out that Esau his brother is a hairy man, which is how Jacob could pass as Esau when deceiving his blind father Isaac. Genesis 27:23 says Isaac did not recognize Jacob because his hands were hairy like Esau's. Genesis 25:25 describes Esau at birth as red and hairy all over, like a garment.

senses.definition: The tragic flaw of the protagonist in a literary tragedy.
senses.example: Creon's main hamartia was his excessive pride.

senses.definition: Sin.
A focal malformation consisting of disorganized arrangement of tissue types.

core.definition: In literary tragedy, the tragic flaw or error in a hero's character that leads to his downfall; in theology, sin.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'TEE,' the third syllable, with a secondary stress on 'HAM.' The 'r' is pronounced clearly, and the final vowel is a soft 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in literary criticism. In theological use it has a serious, negative tone meaning sin.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'hamartia' mostly in literature classes and in writing about Aristotle's Poetics. In everyday speech they would say 'fatal flaw' or 'tragic flaw' instead. In theology, the Greek word is used when discussing the New Testament meaning of sin as missing the mark.

distinctions.note: Tragic flaw is the everyday English phrase for the same literary idea; hamartia is the technical Greek term, used mainly in classical criticism.
Sin is the general term in English for moral wrong; hamartia in the literary sense is an error that leads to tragedy, not necessarily a moral failing.

examples.everyday: In my book club we argued about whether Macbeth's ambition is his tragic flaw, which is what Aristotle would call hamartia.
examples.professional: In the English seminar, the instructor asked us to identify the hamartia in each protagonist before writing the essay.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's hamartia is best understood not as a moral vice but as an error of judgment that the audience can recognize as human, which is what makes the fall tragic.

nuance.analogy: Hamartia is like a crack in a strong vase: the vase may be beautiful, but the flaw is what eventually breaks it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hamartia, missing the mark or error, from hamartanein, to miss the mark.
common_mistakes: Using it as a general word for any mistake; in literature it means a tragic error or flaw.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable instead of 'TEE.'
Confusing it with 'hamartoma,' a medical term for a benign tumor-like growth.
nuance.biblical_note: In the New Testament the Greek word hamartia, meaning missing the mark, is the common word for sin. Romans 3:23 of the RSV says that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God. Romans 6:23 says the wages of sin is death, and John 8:34 says that everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin. The word thus moves from a literary idea of tragic error to a theological idea of sin as a power that enslaves.

hamartia.etymology: From Ancient Greek *ἁμαρτία* (“tragic failure, sinful nature”), from the verb *ἁμαρτάνω* (“to miss the mark”).

senses.definition: Conveying in demeanour the assumption of superiority; disdainful, supercilious.

core.definition: Acting or looking as if you think you are better than others and they are beneath you.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final vowel a clear 'ee'. Do not add a 'gh' sound; the 'gh' is silent, and the vowel is the 'aw' of 'caught'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests disdain and an unpleasant superiority.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'haughty' mainly in descriptions of people's looks, voices or behavior, often in books, reviews or news writing. In everyday speech, 'snobby' or 'stuck-up' is more common. It is not rude to use, but it sounds more formal than most casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Proud can be positive, meaning pleased with an accomplishment, while haughty is always negative and implies looking down on others.
Arrogant is more general and common, while haughty specifically describes a cold, lofty manner of disdain.

examples.everyday: The hostess gave us a haughty look and said the wait would be an hour, even though the place was half empty.
examples.professional: The vendor's haughty replies in the email thread made the whole project team want to switch suppliers.
examples.analytical: Nietzsche often portrays the haughty aristocrat as someone who creates values for himself rather than seeking approval from others.

nuance.analogy: A haughty person is like someone standing on a balcony, looking down at a crowd as if they were not quite worth noticing.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English haute, from Old French haut, meaning high, from Latin altus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a 'ow' sound as in 'how', which changes the word's sound.
Using 'haughty' to mean simply proud or confident in a positive sense.

senses.definition: Grass cut and dried for use as animal fodder.
Any mix of green leafy plants used for fodder.
Cannabis; marijuana.
A net set around the haunt of an animal, especially a rabbit.
The letter for the h sound in Pitman shorthand.
The Latin letter H.
To cut grasses or herb plants for use as animal fodder.
To lay snares for rabbits.

core.definition: Dried grass or other plants cut and stored as food for farm animals such as horses and cows.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long "ay" vowel. Do not add a "y" sound at the end; it is not "hey".

nuance.connotation: Neutral and rural. It is a simple everyday word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "hay" in farm, ranch, and country contexts, and in phrases about horses and barns. Bales of hay are common in fall and summer. In slang, "hay" can also mean marijuana, but this is informal and regional.

distinctions.note: Straw is the dry stalk left after harvest; hay is grass or plants cut and dried for feed.
Grass is growing; hay is cut and dried for storage and feeding.

collocations: make hay while the sun shines

examples.everyday: We need to pick up a few bales of hay before the storm.
examples.professional: The ranch's hay contract was renewed with the local supplier for next season.
examples.analytical: In the parable, the grass and hay represent what is temporary, in contrast to what endures.

nuance.analogy: Hay is like dried leaves stored for winter, ready to feed animals when fresh grass is gone.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hieg, meaning cut grass.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like "hey" with an "h" sound at the end.
Confusing "hay fever" with a fever caused by hay; it is an allergy to pollen.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew chatsir (חָצִיר) means grass or hay, referring to green plants used for food. Psalm 103:15 compares human life to grass and flowers that quickly fade. Proverbs 27:25 describes hay appearing and tender grass shown as part of an ordinary, sustaining harvest. Isaiah 40:6-8 uses the withering of grass as a picture of human frailty, contrasted with the enduring word of God.

hay.etymology: From Middle English *hey*, from Old English *hīeġ*, from **hawi*, from Proto-Germanic **hawją*, from **hawwaną* (“to hew, cut down”).

senses.definition: The state of being heavy; weight, weightiness, force of impact or gravity.

core.definition: The quality of being heavy in weight, or the feeling of sadness, sluggishness, or weight in the body or mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the next two syllables are quick and reduced. Don't add a long 'ee' to the middle syllable or pronounce the ending as 'ness' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing weight; negative when describing sadness or heaviness of mood.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use heaviness for physical weight or for a heavy feeling in the chest or limbs, as in 'a heaviness in my legs.' For emotional sadness, they often prefer heaviness of heart in literary contexts, or simply sadness or grief in everyday speech. It sounds slightly literary in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Weight is the measurable mass, while heaviness can describe the felt sense of weight or sadness.
Sadness is the common everyday word for unhappiness, while heaviness describes a weighed-down feeling in the body or heart.

examples.everyday: After the long flight I felt a heaviness in my legs that wouldn't go away.
examples.professional: The heaviness of the project backlog has made the whole team tired and slow this quarter.
examples.analytical: Scripture often names heaviness of heart not as a sin in itself but as a condition that calls for hope in God.

nuance.analogy: Heaviness is like wet clothing that clings and drags you down, making every step harder.
nuance.etymology: From heavy, from Old English hefig, plus the suffix -ness, meaning 'the state of being'.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle syllable with a long vowel, as in HEV-ee-nus.
Using heaviness for a heavy object, where weight or heavy is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In older English translations, heaviness can mean grief or sorrow of the spirit, which the RSV usually renders as anguish, sorrow, or a downcast heart. Proverbs 12:25 says that anxiety in a man's heart weighs him down, while a good word cheers him. The passage shows that inner heaviness is real and that encouraging words can lift it.

heaviness.etymology: From Middle English *hevynesse*, from Old English *hefiġnes* (“heaviness”).

senses.definition: To mark (important passages of text), e.g. with a fluorescent marker pen or in a wordprocessor, as a means of memory retention or for later reference.
To make prominent; emphasize.
To be a highlight of.
To dye (part of the hair) a different color than the rest.
To seek the attention of (a user) on IRC by mentioning their name in a message, causing that message to appear highlighted on their screen.
An area or a spot in a drawing, painting, or photograph that is strongly illuminated.
An especially significant or interesting detail or event or period of time.
senses.example: Meeting my future wife was the highlight of my trip to Spain.

senses.definition: A strand or spot of hair dyed a different color than the rest.

core.definition: To mark important text, usually with a colored marker, or to draw special attention to something as important.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HY, and the second syllable rhymes with 'light' with a final t. Avoid adding an extra vowel at the end, as in 'high-lite-uh'.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans commonly say highlight the important part when marking text, slides, or spreadsheets, and highlight a point in meetings to draw attention to it. As a noun, a highlight is the best part of an event or a show, especially in sports reporting. It is informal enough for everyday talk and standard in work settings.

distinctions.note: Emphasize means to stress a point in speech or writing; highlight can also mean marking text or drawing attention to something visually.
Underline draws a line under words, while highlight usually means coloring the background of text, often with a marker or software tool.

examples.everyday: Can you highlight the best parts of the recipe so we don't miss anything when we shop tomorrow?
examples.professional: Let's highlight the three main risks at the top of the slide so leadership sees them first.
examples.analytical: The author highlights the tension between individual conscience and communal obligation, which becomes central to her argument.

nuance.analogy: Highlighting is like turning on a flashlight in a dark room: it makes certain parts of the text or idea impossible to miss.
nuance.etymology: From high + light, originally from painting, meaning the brightest area of a picture.
common_mistakes: Using 'highlight' for 'hyperlink' or 'link' when talking about web pages.
Saying 'highlight it up' instead of simply 'highlight it'.

conversation.text: I didn't watch the game, but I saw the highlights.
The highlight of the trip was the Grand Canyon.
Highlight the important parts with a yellow marker.

senses.definition: A main public road, especially a multi-lane, high-speed thoroughfare.
Any public road.
A way; a path that leads to a certain destiny.
senses.example: You're on a highway to greatness.

senses.definition: Synonym of bus (“common connection for two or more circuits or components”).
To travel on a highway.

core.definition: A large public road, usually with several lanes and fast traffic, connecting cities or regions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HY, and the second syllable is a diphthong like 'way'. Keep the first vowel long and clear, and don't add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use highway for major roads between cities, often with numbers such as Highway 101. Freeway is common in California and some western cities, and interstate refers to the federal system. Expressway is used for limited-access roads in many regions.

distinctions.note: Freeway is common in some American regions for a limited-access highway with no traffic lights, while highway is the more general term.
Road is any public way; highway suggests a major route for longer-distance travel.

examples.everyday: We took the highway to Chicago, so the drive only took about four hours.
examples.professional: The client's office is right off the highway, so the team can reach the site in fifteen minutes.
examples.analytical: The new highway system transformed American travel by linking distant towns into a national network.

nuance.analogy: A highway is like a main artery in a body: a large route that carries most of the traffic between major areas.
nuance.etymology: From high + way, originally meaning a main public road.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in the highway' instead of 'on the highway', which is the normal American preposition.
Using highway for a short residential street.

highway.etymology: From Middle English *heiȝwai*, *heiȝwei*, from Old English *hēahweġ* (“main road, highway”), corresponding to *high* + *way*.

conversation.text: Take the highway; it's much faster than the back roads.
There's a rest stop off the highway about thirty miles from here.
The speed limit on this highway is seventy.

senses.definition: Not friendly; appropriate to an enemy; showing the disposition of an enemy; showing ill will and malevolence or a desire to thwart and injure.
senses.example: a hostile force

senses.definition: Aggressive; antagonistic.
Unwilling.
Being or relating to a hostile takeover.
senses.example: Microsoft may go hostile in its bid for Yahoo! as soon as Friday, according to a published report.

senses.definition: An enemy.

core.definition: Showing open opposition, dislike, or ill will; unfriendly, or acting like an enemy toward someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel, so it sounds like HAH-stul, with no clear i or ee sound. Do not confuse it with hostility, where the stress moves to the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes active opposition or unfriendliness, and it can be strong in both casual and serious contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hostile for people who are openly unfriendly, for environments that feel threatening, and for political or military opposition. In everyday talk, unfriendly or cold is softer, so hostile sounds strong. Hostile environment is a common phrase in workplace and policy discussions.

distinctions.note: Unfriendly is milder and can mean merely cool or distant, while hostile implies active ill will or opposition.
Antagonistic suggests an opposing or argumentative stance, often in a dispute, and it is less emotionally charged than hostile.

examples.everyday: My neighbor has been pretty hostile about the parking since we moved in.
examples.professional: The meeting turned hostile when the budget cuts were announced, and nobody wanted to compromise.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the early church's hostile reception from the surrounding culture shaped its theology of martyrdom.

nuance.analogy: A hostile environment is like a cold wind that pushes back against everything you try to do.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin hostilis, from Latin hostis, enemy.
common_mistakes: Using hostile for mild dislike, which sounds too strong.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a clear ee sound, as in HAH-stee-ul.

hostile.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *hostile*, from Latin *hostīlis*, from *hostis* (“enemy”).

senses.definition: Having been subject to propaganda and promotion; promoted beyond what is reasonable or appropriate.
Excited.
senses.example: He's hyped about getting to kiss her in the final scene of the play.

core.definition: Very excited and eager about something coming up, or promoted with exaggerated publicity beyond what it deserves.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable, ending with a crisp 't' sound. Do not add an extra 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive in casual talk when it means excited, and skeptical when it means overpromoted. Context decides which.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm so hyped' to express excitement, especially about sports, concerts, or trips. They also use 'overhyped' to say something was promoted too much. The word is very casual, so avoid it in formal writing.

distinctions.note: Excited is neutral and works in all contexts, while hyped is casual and often implies pumped-up energy.
Hyped can be positive, but overhyped always signals disappointment or doubt.

examples.everyday: Our whole family is hyped for the Fourth of July fireworks this year.
examples.professional: The product launch was hyped so heavily that expectations became impossible to meet.
examples.analytical: The hyped promises of the early internet era show how publicity can outrun the evidence.

nuance.analogy: A hyped person is like a battery running at full charge, full of energy and ready to go.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of 'hype', from the noun 'hype', origin uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using 'hyped' in formal writing, where 'excited' or 'overpromoted' is safer.
Saying 'I am hype' instead of 'I am hyped'.

conversation.text: I'm so hyped for the concert tonight!
The kids are hyped about Halloween.
Everybody was hyped for the game, but it was a blowout.

senses.definition: A conic section formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane that intersects the base of the cone and is not tangent to the cone. The function y(x) = 1/x draws a hyperbola.

core.definition: A curve in mathematics made of two separate branches, formed by slicing a double cone with a plane, or defined by a constant difference of distances from two foci.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, -PUR-, not the first. The middle syllables are reduced and quick, and the final 'a' is a soft 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hyperbola in math and science classes, engineering, and physics. It is precise and not used in casual talk. Students often confuse it with parabola, so be careful in exams and technical writing.

distinctions.note: A parabola has one branch and a single focus, while a hyperbola has two branches and two foci.
An ellipse is a closed curve, while a hyperbola is open and has two separate branches.

examples.everyday: The cover of my old calculus book had a graph of a hyperbola in bright blue.
examples.professional: The sensor's response curve follows a hyperbola, so we fit it with a hyperbolic function.
examples.analytical: A hyperbola is the set of points whose distances to two fixed foci differ by a constant amount.

nuance.analogy: A hyperbola is like two mirror-image arches that open away from each other, never meeting.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hyperbolē, 'excess' or 'throwing beyond', used by Apollonius for this curve.
common_mistakes: Confusing hyperbola with parabola in exams or math discussions.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'HY-per-bo-la'.

hyperbola.etymology: From New Latin *hyperbola*, from Ancient Greek *ὑπερβολή*.

senses.definition: Saying you didn't reach your connecting flight in time.

core.definition: Saying you did not reach your connecting flight, train or bus in time, so you need to rebook.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'nek' in 'connection.' Reduce the 'o' sound in 'connection' to a quick schwa, and do not pronounce the 'ct' as a separate hard sound.

nuance.connotation: negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at an airport gate, to an airline agent, or to someone waiting for you. It usually comes with a request, such as 'Can you rebook me?' It is neutral and polite. Use 'connecting flight' or 'connection' interchangeably in air travel.

distinctions.note: 'Missed my flight' means you did not board the flight at all, while 'missed my connection' means you missed the second leg of a trip.

collocations: I missed my connection in Chicago
I missed my connection because the first flight was late
Can you help me rebook my connection?

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, I missed my connection in Denver.
examples.professional: I missed my connection, so I'll join the client call remotely from the airport.
examples.analytical: A delayed first leg means the passenger misses the connection, which shifts the entire itinerary.

nuance.analogy: Like missing the last train that would take you the final stretch of a journey.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I lost my connection' for a missed flight, which means something else in American English
Pronouncing 'connection' with a heavy stress on the final syllable

conversation.text: I missed my connection in Atlanta, so I'm on the next flight.
My first flight landed late, and I missed my connection.
"Where are you?" "Still in Dallas. I missed my connection."

senses.definition: In a manner that produces illegible results.
senses.example: The doctor illegibly scrawled his signature: if it weren't on his letterhead, no-one would know who had written it.

core.definition: In a way that is hard or impossible to read.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, LEJ. The final '-ly' is a clear 'lee', and the middle syllable is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: negative. It describes writing that is hard to read, often with mild criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'illegibly' mostly to describe how something was written or printed, such as 'the form was filled out illegibly'. In speech people more often say 'I can't read your writing' or 'it's hard to make out'. It is common in forms, instructions and notes.

distinctions.note: 'Badly' is general and can describe any poor quality; 'illegibly' is specifically about readability.

examples.everyday: Your grandma wrote the recipe so illegibly that I had to guess the amount of sugar.
examples.professional: Please don't submit the form if the box is filled out illegibly, because the system will reject it.
examples.analytical: The document was copied illegibly, so the textual variants cannot be confirmed with any confidence.

nuance.analogy: Writing illegibly is like speaking so quietly and quickly that no one can make out a word.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'illegible' plus the adverb suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'illegibly' for people who are hard to understand; it refers only to writing.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ih-LEG-uh-blee, which sounds too harsh and unnatural.

senses.definition: To move into a foreign country in order to reside there permanently.

core.definition: To move from your own country to another country in order to live there permanently.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, IM-. Say the middle syllable as a quick reduced uh, and do not add an extra syllable before the t. Keep the r in grayt clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a move without judging it, though news and politics often use it with strong feelings attached.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use immigrate for a permanent move into the country, usually when talking about family history, policy or legal status. For a temporary stay, people say move abroad or work overseas. You often hear the phrase immigrate to the United States, and the person is called an immigrant. Do not confuse it with emigrate, which describes leaving a country.

distinctions.note: Immigrate describes arriving in a new country; emigrate describes leaving your home country. The same move is both: a person emigrates from Mexico and immigrates to the US.
Move is general and can be temporary or local; immigrate always means settling permanently in a foreign country.

examples.everyday: My grandparents immigrated to Ohio in 1952 with almost nothing, so I grew up hearing their stories.
examples.professional: Our HR team confirmed that the new engineer will immigrate on a work visa and needs relocation support.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate why some groups chose to immigrate during periods of economic upheaval while others remained in place.

nuance.analogy: Immigrating is like a plant being transplanted into new soil: it arrives somewhere new and is expected to take root there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin immigrare, to move into, from in- (into) and migrare (to move).
common_mistakes: Using immigrate for leaving a country; that is emigrate, so say I emigrated from Brazil, not I immigrated from Brazil.
Adding a preposition after the verb in the wrong place, for example immigrate in the US; use immigrate to the US.

immigrate.etymology: From Latin *immigratus*, past participle of *immigro* (“remove, move into”).

senses.definition: Impossible to permeate.
Not allowing passage, especially of liquids; waterproof.

core.definition: Not allowing liquids, gases, or other substances to pass through; waterproof or sealed against passage.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUR, and the -mea- part is pronounced as 'mee' with a reduced final vowel. The ending -able is weak, so say 'uh-bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical property, but it can also sound metaphorical when used for a person or a boundary that cannot be penetrated.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people more often say 'waterproof' or 'watertight' for things like jackets or containers. 'Impermeable' is common in science, engineering, medicine, and architecture. It can also be used figuratively for a mind or barrier that cannot be reached.

distinctions.note: Waterproof is everyday and applies to clothing, shoes, or equipment. Impermeable is more technical and can apply to membranes, rock, or gases.

Impenetrable means impossible to enter or pass through physically or mentally, and it can describe a dense crowd or a difficult text. Impermeable focuses on fluids or substances passing through a surface.

examples.everyday: Get a jacket that's impermeable to rain, because the forecast says it's going to pour.
examples.professional: The contractor recommended an impermeable liner under the parking lot to protect the groundwater.
examples.analytical: The author treats the self as an impermeable boundary, one that outside influences cannot penetrate.

nuance.analogy: Like a plastic bag that keeps water from leaking through, an impermeable material holds back whatever tries to pass through it.
nuance.etymology: From im- (not) plus permeable, from Latin permeare (to pass through).
common_mistakes: Using the preposition 'of' instead of 'to', as in 'impermeable of water'.
Confusing 'impermeable' with 'impermeability' in spoken sentences, where a noun is needed.

senses.definition: Not coherent.
senses.example: When we confronted her, she gave us a hasty, incoherent explanation.

senses.definition: Not making logical sense; not logically connected or consistent.
senses.example: When we confronted her, she gave us a hasty, incoherent explanation.

senses.definition: Not cohering socially, not united.

core.definition: Not making logical sense, or having parts that do not connect clearly to one another.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HEER, and the last syllable is a weak uhnt, not ent. The r is pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes speech or writing that lacks sense, and can describe a person who is confused or delirious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use incoherent for a rambling speech, a text message written in a rush, or someone who is very drunk or ill. For a person it can sound harsh, so 'she was rambling' is often kinder in conversation. In professional writing it is a precise criticism of an argument.

distinctions.note: Illogical means it breaks rules of reasoning, while incoherent means it does not hang together as a whole.
Unclear means hard to understand, while incoherent means the content itself does not connect logically.

examples.everyday: He was so tired after the flight that his answers came out incoherent.
examples.professional: Your email is incoherent, so could you rewrite the summary with the three decisions in order?
examples.analytical: Without a shared account of truth, the argument becomes incoherent, since each premise assumes a standard the conclusion rejects.

nuance.analogy: Like a puzzle whose pieces are all there but do not fit together into a picture.
nuance.etymology: From Latin incohaerens, from in- 'not' plus cohaerere 'to stick together'.
common_mistakes: Saying incoherent with the stress on the first syllable.
Using incoherent for an unclear word; it means the whole thing lacks logical connection.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being incomprehensible.
Something that cannot be understood.

core.definition: The quality of being impossible to understand fully; in theology, the doctrine that God's nature exceeds the human mind's grasp.

pronunciation.tip: A long word with primary stress on BIL near the end and secondary stresses earlier. Say the middle clearly, 'hen-suh,' and flap the final t to sound like 'dee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theology, where it expresses reverence. In ordinary use it is negative, describing confusing or unclear writing or speech.
nuance.usage_note: In theology, it refers to God's being beyond complete human understanding, not to something absurd or irrational. In ordinary American use it describes things that are confusing, such as legal language. Many speakers prefer simpler words like 'confusing' or 'unintelligibility.'

distinctions.note: Unintelligibility usually means speech or writing that cannot be made out; incomprehensibility suggests something that cannot be grasped by the mind.
Ineffability means that something cannot be expressed in words; incomprehensibility means it cannot be fully understood.
Mystery is the broader and warmer word; incomprehensibility is the technical term for the limit of understanding.

examples.everyday: The incomprehensibility of the instructions made me give up on assembling the shelf.
examples.professional: The contract's incomprehensibility to ordinary customers led our legal team to rewrite it in plain English.
examples.analytical: Gregory of Nyssa teaches that God's incomprehensibility is not a failure of faith but the very condition of endless spiritual ascent.

nuance.analogy: Like trying to pour the ocean into a teacup: you can touch the ocean, but the cup cannot hold it.
nuance.etymology: From incomprehensible, from Latin incomprehensibilis, 'that cannot be grasped,' from in- + comprehendere, 'to seize.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'incomprehension,' which means failure to understand.
Misplacing stress by saying in-com-pre-HEN-si-bil-i-ty with the main stress too early.
nuance.biblical_note: Romans 11:33 exclaims that God's judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable. Isaiah 55:8-9 says God's thoughts and ways are higher than human thoughts and ways. Job 11:7 asks whether one can find out the deep things of God.

traditions.view: God's essence is utterly unknowable, while his energies can be experienced. This apophatic emphasis is central to Orthodox mysticism and the Cappadocian Fathers.
God can be truly known but never comprehended; Thomas Aquinas and the Fourth Lateran Council affirm that God is ineffable and exceeds the intellect.
Reformed theology stresses that God is knowable only as he reveals himself, so human knowledge is analogical and never exhaustive. Lutherans speak of the hidden God (Deus absconditus).

senses.definition: The quality or state of being independent; lack of dependence; the state of not being reliant on, or controlled by, others.
senses.example: In 1947, India gained independence from the British Empire.

senses.definition: The state of having sufficient means for a comfortable livelihood.

core.definition: In statistics, the property that knowing one event or variable gives no information about another.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on PEN. The final -ence is reduced to a soft 'uhns,' not a full 'ens.'

nuance.connotation: Positive in everyday life, meaning freedom and self-reliance. In statistics it is neutral and precise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word everywhere, from Independence Day to personal freedom and financial self-sufficiency. In data science, 'independence' is a technical property that must be checked before using certain tests. In everyday talk, a natural phrase is 'she wants more independence.'

distinctions.note: Freedom is the absence of external constraint, while independence can also mean self-reliance or not depending on others.
Dependence is reliance on something or someone, the opposite of independence.

examples.everyday: After she moved out and paid her own rent, she finally felt a real sense of independence.
examples.professional: Before we run the chi-square test, we need to check the independence of the observations.
examples.analytical: Statistical independence is a precise condition that cannot be inferred from correlation alone.

nuance.analogy: Like two people walking on separate paths: each moves on its own, and one's step tells you nothing about the other's.
nuance.etymology: From Latin independere, 'not to depend,' from in- 'not' and dependere 'to hang from.'
common_mistakes: Using 'independence' for 'independent' in a sentence, as in 'the independence team.'
Confusing statistical independence with having no relationship at all.

senses.definition: Harmless; producing no ill effect.
Inoffensive; unprovocative; unexceptionable.

core.definition: Harmless; not likely to cause offense, injury, or trouble. Often describes something that looks like it could be a problem but isn't.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NAHK. The middle syllable is quick and light, almost 'yuh', so the word has three syllables, not four.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive: it describes something that seems risky or offensive but turns out harmless. It can also sound like faint praise when used of a person's remarks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in news, medicine, legal, and professional writing, such as 'an innocuous side effect' or 'an innocuous comment in the meeting.' In casual speech people usually say 'harmless' or 'no big deal' instead. Using it in a conversation is fine but may sound a bit stiff.

distinctions.note: Harmless is everyday and general; innocuous is more formal and often implies that something looks suspicious or offensive but isn't.
Innocent describes a person who has not done wrong or a lack of knowledge; innocuous describes things, remarks, or substances that do no damage.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about that rash, the doctor said it's innocuous and will go away in a few days.
examples.professional: The email looked innocuous, but the security team flagged the attachment for review.
examples.analytical: Many arguments that seem innocuous at first conceal premises that carry significant moral weight.

nuance.analogy: Like a house cat that looks fierce but is actually harmless.
nuance.etymology: From Latin innocuus, 'not harmful,' from in- 'not' plus nocere 'to harm.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'innocent' when describing a thing rather than a person.
Pronouncing it with a stressed final syllable or dropping the middle 'yoo' sound.

senses.definition: The faculty of thinking, judging, abstract reasoning, and conceptual understanding; the cognitive faculty.
senses.example: Intellect is one of man's greatest powers.

senses.definition: The capacity of that faculty (in a particular person).
senses.example: They were chosen because of their outstanding intellect.

senses.definition: A person who has that faculty to a great degree.
senses.example: Some of the world's leading intellects were meeting there.

core.definition: The mental capacity to think, reason, understand ideas, and make judgments; the power of the mind to know.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, IN. The second syllable is a reduced schwa, so say 'in-tuh-lekt' quickly, not 'in-tel-ect' with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It usually praises someone's mental power, but calling a person 'an intellect' can sound slightly formal or grand.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intellect mostly in writing, academic discussion, or formal speech about the mind, as in 'a mind of great intellect.' In everyday conversation people usually say 'smart' or 'brains' instead. Saying someone is 'a great intellect' is a compliment that sounds a bit lofty, so it fits a eulogy, a review, or a serious discussion.

distinctions.note: Intelligence is the general ability to learn and solve problems; intellect is more about the mind's power of abstract thought and reasoning.
Intellectual is an adjective (an intellectual discussion) or a person who enjoys ideas; intellect is the faculty itself.
Mind is the whole conscious life of thought and feeling; intellect is specifically the reasoning and understanding part.

examples.everyday: My grandfather had a sharp intellect right up until the end, and he still beat everyone at chess.
examples.professional: The hiring committee was looking for a candidate with a strong intellect and the ability to work across teams.
examples.analytical: Augustine argues that the intellect can grasp eternal truths only when it is illuminated by God, not by its own unaided power.

nuance.analogy: The intellect is like a lens that focuses scattered light into a clear image; it gathers facts and brings them into sharp, usable understanding.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intellectus, 'understanding,' from intellegere, 'to perceive, understand,' from inter- and legere, 'to choose, read.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'in-tel-ECT' with stress on the last syllable.
Using intellect as a verb or adjective; the adjective is intellectual.
Treating intellect and intelligence as always interchangeable in everyday speech.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word nous, often translated mind or understanding, names the faculty by which a person perceives and judges spiritually as well as intellectually. Romans 12:2 speaks of being transformed by the renewal of the mind, so that one can discern God's will. Mark 12:30 records Jesus quoting the command to love the Lord with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength, which includes the intellect as part of wholehearted devotion.

intellect.etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin *intellēctus* (“understanding, intellect”), from Latin *intellegō* (“understand; reason”), from *inter* (“between, among”) + *legō* (“read”), with connotation of bind.

senses.definition: To plead on someone else's behalf.
senses.example: Our Lady intercedes

senses.definition: To act as a mediator in a dispute; to arbitrate or mediate.
To pass between; to intervene.

core.definition: To speak or plead for someone else, often to a person with power to help or to settle a dispute.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the final syllable, -SEED. The t is flapped in American speech, so it sounds like 'in-der-SEED', not 'in-ter-SEE-ded'.

nuance.connotation: positive or neutral; it implies helping someone with a plea or a good word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intercede in formal speech and writing, such as a manager speaking for an employee or a diplomat stepping in. In everyday talk they say 'put in a good word for' or 'stick up for someone'. Do not use it for an ordinary interruption.

distinctions.note: Intervene means to step into a situation, often forcefully; intercede means to speak on someone else's behalf.
Mediate means to help two sides reach agreement as a neutral party; intercede means to advocate for one party.
Plead means to beg directly; intercede means to ask on someone else's behalf.

examples.everyday: Could you intercede with the landlord for me? He never answers my calls.
examples.professional: Our VP agreed to intercede with legal so the contract could be approved this week.
examples.analytical: Locke's account of the state of nature assumes that a neutral judge must intercede when private disputes escalate.

nuance.analogy: Like a friend who walks into the principal's office to speak up for you while you wait outside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intercedere, 'to come between, intervene', from inter, 'between', and cedere, 'to go'.
common_mistakes: Using 'intercede to' instead of 'intercede with' or 'intercede on behalf of'.
Stressing the first syllable; the stress belongs on -SEED.

senses.definition: The state of being intolerant.
senses.example: Religious intolerance is a serious problem in Brazil.

senses.definition: Extreme sensitivity to a food or drug; of a food that is generally considered edible, an individual inability to digest it.
senses.example: lactose intolerance

core.definition: Unwillingness to accept beliefs, opinions, or groups that differ from your own; also an inability to digest certain foods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAH. The -ance ending is pronounced 'uns' in American speech, and the r is clearly sounded.

nuance.connotation: negative; intolerance is usually seen as a flaw, though 'lactose intolerance' is a neutral medical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use intolerance most for religious, political, or social unwillingness to accept others. For food, they say 'lactose intolerance' or 'gluten intolerance', which is different from a food allergy. A natural reply to a claim of intolerance is 'Let's talk about it.'

distinctions.note: Bigotry is stronger, meaning hatred based on prejudice; intolerance is more general refusal to accept differences.
An allergy is an immune reaction; food intolerance is a digestive problem without immune involvement.

examples.everyday: I have lactose intolerance, so I always ask for oat milk.
examples.professional: We need to address intolerance in code reviews, where comments sometimes get personal.
examples.analytical: Historians trace the rise of religious intolerance in early modern Europe to the breakdown of shared political authority.

nuance.analogy: Intolerance is like a door that will open only for people who already look like you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin intolerantia, from intolerans 'not enduring', from in- 'not' + tolerare 'to bear'.
common_mistakes: Using intolerance for a food allergy; use 'allergy' for immune reactions.
Stressing the middle syllable; keep the main stress on TAH.

intolerance.etymology: French *intolérance*, itself from *in-* + *tolérance* or borrowed from Latin *intolerantia* (“insolence, insufferableness; intolerance”).

senses.definition: Very curious and interested in something because it seems unusual or mysterious.

core.definition: Very curious and interested in something because it seems unusual or mysterious.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, in-TREEGD, not on the first as the dictionary suggests. The ending -ed is pronounced as a plain d after g.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes curiosity and engagement, which Americans generally find attractive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I'm intrigued' or 'I'm intrigued by' to signal polite interest in an idea, offer, or proposal without committing. It is friendly and professional, suitable for meetings and casual talk alike.

distinctions.note: Curious is broader and can mean simply wanting to know; intrigued implies that something has caught your attention in an appealing way.
Interested is more neutral and can be mild; intrigued suggests stronger, more puzzled attention.

examples.everyday: Your friend says he wants to open a food truck, and I'm intrigued by the idea.
examples.professional: I'm intrigued by your proposal to reduce model training time, so let's set up a call next week.
examples.analytical: Readers are intrigued by the narrator's silences, which invite them to supply the missing motives themselves.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat that hears an unusual sound: its ears turn and it leans forward to find out what it is.
nuance.etymology: From the verb intrigue, from French intriguer, 'to puzzle or fascinate'.
common_mistakes: Using 'intrigued' to mean 'intriguing'; say 'The idea is intriguing' but 'I am intrigued'.
Following 'intrigued' with 'of' instead of 'by'; the usual American form is 'intrigued by'.

conversation.text: I was intrigued by the menu, so we decided to try it.
She looked intrigued when I mentioned the job opening.
I'm intrigued. Tell me more about this mystery trip.

senses.definition: The ninth letter of the Greek alphabet (Ι, ι).
senses.example: As a Greek numeral, iota represents ten.

senses.definition: The Latin letter Ɩ (minuscule: ɩ).
A jot; a very small, insignificant quantity.

core.definition: A very small amount; the tiniest bit of something, usually used in negative phrases.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'OH', the second syllable. The first syllable rhymes with 'eye', and the final vowel is a reduced 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is most often used in negative phrases, which give it a sense of emphasis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use 'iota' in the phrase 'not an iota', as in 'there isn't an iota of evidence.' It sounds slightly formal or emphatic. In casual talk, people often say 'not a bit' or 'not one bit' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Jot' is nearly identical in meaning but more casual; 'iota' sounds a bit more formal.
'Bit' is a general, everyday word for a small amount; 'iota' is stronger and usually used in negative phrases.

examples.everyday: I don't have an iota of patience left after that traffic jam.
examples.professional: The data shows not an iota of improvement after the patch.
examples.analytical: The argument offers not an iota of evidence for its central claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a single grain of sand on a beach: real, but almost impossible to notice.
nuance.etymology: From Greek iota, the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, the smallest letter in Greek.
common_mistakes: Use 'iota' without a negative in casual speech, where it can sound oddly formal.
Stress the first syllable; the stress falls on the second syllable, 'OH'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Greek of Matthew 5:18 (RSV), 'iota' names the smallest letter of the Greek alphabet, which translates the Hebrew yodh, the smallest Hebrew letter. Jesus says that not an iota or a dot will pass from the law until all is accomplished, emphasizing the smallest details of the law.

senses.definition: The name of several priests in the Bible, especially a priestly family that returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel.

core.definition: The name of several priests in the Bible, especially a priestly family that returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'DAY'. The final syllable is a light 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans see this name in Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles, mostly in Bible study or reference works. You will not use it in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Jeshua is a different name, belonging to the high priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, while Jedaiah names a priestly family and several individuals.

examples.everyday: My friend asked who Jedaiah was, and I told her he was one of the priests who came back from exile.
examples.professional: In my workshop on post-exilic history, I listed the families of Jedaiah among the returning priests in Ezra and Nehemiah.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists of priestly families such as Jedaiah's in Nehemiah 12 show how the post-exilic community tied its worship to lineage.

nuance.analogy: Think of Jedaiah as a family name on a membership roll, showing who belonged to which group when the community returned home.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yedayah, meaning Yahweh knows.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in JED-ay-uh.
Confusing Jedaiah with Jediael, a different name in Chronicles.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Yedayah means Yahweh knows. Ezra 2:36 lists the sons of Jedaiah among the priests who returned from exile. Nehemiah 7:39 gives a similar list. Nehemiah 12:6-7 names a Jedaiah among the priests and Levites of the time of Joiakim, son of Jeshua, the high priest, showing the priestly families continuing after the return.

senses.definition: A king of Judah, son of Asa, remembered for seeking the LORD and reforming worship, and the name of a valley linked with divine judgment in Joel.

core.definition: A king of Judah, son of Asa, remembered for seeking the LORD and reforming worship, and the name of a valley linked with divine judgment in Joel.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HAH, and the final syllable is 'fat', with a short a. The middle syllables are reduced, so the word sounds like 'jih-HAH-shuh-fat'.

nuance.connotation: positive; he is praised for faithfulness in the biblical narrative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name in Bible study, sermons and church settings, and also when naming the valley in Joel. People outside the church often know the name from its use as a surname. It is written with a capital letter and needs no article.

distinctions.note: Jehoram was the son of Jehoshaphat, a different king who was judged negatively, so the two names should be kept distinct.

examples.everyday: My grandmother named her cat Jehoshaphat, which is a name you do not hear every day.
examples.professional: In the Old Testament survey, I used Jehoshaphat's reform to show how a king can strengthen the courts and teaching of the law.
examples.analytical: Jehoshaphat's prayer in 2 Chronicles 20 depicts a dependence on God that contrasts with reliance on military alliances.

nuance.analogy: Like a wise judge who restores the courts so that justice can be done fairly.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Yəhôšāp̄āṭ, meaning 'Yahweh judges'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, which sounds unnatural.
Pronouncing the sh as 's' or dropping the middle syllables entirely.
nuance.biblical_note: Jehoshaphat was a king of Judah who sought the LORD and removed some of the high places, and he sent officials to teach the law throughout the land. The 2 Chronicles account describes his prayer of trust when the nations came against Judah. The prophet Joel also names a valley of Jehoshaphat, where God gathers the nations for judgment.

jehoshaphat.etymology: From Hebrew *יְהוֹשָׁפָט‬*, from *יהוה* + *שָׁפַט*, meaning "Yahweh has judged".

senses.definition: A Hebrew personal name borne by several minor men in the Old Testament; one appears among the men who put away foreign wives in Ezra's time.

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name borne by several minor men in the Old Testament; one appears among the men who put away foreign wives in Ezra's time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the first vowel is a short 'eh', not 'ee'. The final 'th' is voiceless, as in 'math'.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a proper name, so Americans use it only when discussing Bible passages, genealogies or biblical study. It is not a common given name in the United States, so you will rarely hear it outside church or academic settings.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got stuck on a list of names, and somebody asked who Jeremoth was.
examples.professional: In my commentary notes I flagged Jeremoth in Ezra 10 as one of the men listed among those who had married foreign wives.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists in Ezra 10 name Jeremoth among the returnees, and the exegete must decide whether the list preserves a historical record or a later editorial summary.

nuance.analogy: Like a name in a long roll call: he matters to the record even though the story gives him only a line.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Yirmot, a variant of names built on the root for 'high' or 'exalted' (Yarom-type forms; the exact root is debated).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (jer-uh-MOTH); the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the final 'th' as 'd' or 't'.
nuance.biblical_note: Several men named Jeremoth appear in the Old Testament, mostly in Chronicles and Ezra. Ezra 10:26 lists one among the men who had taken foreign wives and agreed to put them away. The name is not tied to any major narrative, so the passage is the main reference.

senses.definition: A Hebrew commander in the Bible, the nephew of King David, who led David's army and was known for both loyalty and brutal killings.

core.definition: A Hebrew commander in the Bible, the nephew of King David, who led David's army and was known for both loyalty and brutal killings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the J is the English j sound. The final b is a clear voiced b, not a soft flap.

nuance.connotation: neutral; the name carries biblical weight, and Joab's story is violent and ambiguous.
nuance.usage_note: Joab is used mainly in Bible study, sermons and discussions of the Old Testament. Americans say it as JOH-ab. In conversation, saying 'Joab' is enough for a Bible-literate listener, and others will ask who he is.

examples.everyday: My cousin named her new baby Joab, and I had to look up where the name comes from.
examples.professional: In Thursday's Bible class we compared how Joab and his brother Abishai served David.
examples.analytical: Joab's murders of Abner and Amasa complicate any reading that presents David's kingship as untouched by violence.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yo'av, meaning 'Yahweh is father'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (joe-AB) instead of the first, JOH-ab.
nuance.biblical_note: Joab, son of Zeruiah, was David's nephew and commander of his army. 2 Samuel 3:22-27 describes his murder of Abner in revenge for the death of his brother Asahel. 2 Samuel 18:14-15 tells how he killed Absalom despite David's wishes. 1 Kings 2:28-34 recounts his death at Solomon's command after he had sided with Adonijah.

senses.definition: A son of Eber in Genesis 10, brother of Peleg and ancestor of several Arabian peoples in the Table of Nations.

core.definition: A son of Eber in Genesis 10, brother of Peleg and ancestor of several Arabian peoples in the Table of Nations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'o' is the short vowel of 'hop', and the final syllable is a reduced schwa with a light 'n'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a proper name with no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this name mainly in Bible study, church teaching, and biblical or ancient Near Eastern scholarship. In everyday talk you would rarely use it. Say 'the descendants of Joktan' rather than inventing new forms of the name.

distinctions.note: Peleg is Joktan's older brother in Genesis 10:25, while Joktan is listed among the sons of Eber in the verses that follow.
Eber is Joktan's father and the ancestor from whom the Hebrews are named in Genesis 10:21 and 10:25.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent ten minutes on Joktan's descendants in Genesis 10.
examples.professional: In my sermon series on the Table of Nations, I placed Joktan's line beside Peleg's to show how the families spread.
examples.analytical: The Table of Nations ties Joktan to peoples of South Arabia, though scholarly identifications of his sons remain debated.

nuance.analogy: Like a branch on a family tree that is listed right next to the line the story follows more closely.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew Yoqtan, a name of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable; the name is stressed on the first syllable.
Confusing Joktan with Jonathan, which is a different biblical name.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Yoqtan (יָקְטָן), a name of uncertain meaning. Genesis 10:25-30 lists Joktan's sons as the ancestors of peoples in South Arabia and beyond, placed beside his brother Peleg. 1 Chronicles 1:19-23 repeats this genealogy in summary form, confirming Joktan as the son of Eber whose sons settled widely. Genesis 10:26-29 names specific sons, such as Sheba and Ophir, whose identifications with later places are discussed by scholars.

senses.definition: The short New Testament letter written by Jude, a brother of James and of Jesus, warning against false teachers.

core.definition: The short New Testament letter written by Jude, a brother of James and of Jesus, warning against false teachers.

pronunciation.tip: Jude is one syllable and rhymes with food. Do not add a vowel between the j and the d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in religious contexts it is a respectful reference to a biblical book or author.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, Jude most often means the New Testament book or the apostle, usually heard in church or Bible study. Outside religion, the name is a common given name for men, so context matters. Americans may refer to the book as the Letter of Jude or simply Jude.

distinctions.note: Judas is the disciple who betrayed Jesus, while Jude is a different apostle and the author of the letter.

examples.everyday: Our pastor's sermon this week came from Jude, and I was surprised how short the book is.
examples.professional: For the seminary syllabus, the Epistle of Jude is paired with 2 Peter because of their shared warnings.
examples.analytical: Jude's letter draws heavily on traditions about fallen angels and cites ancient Jewish texts in its polemic.

nuance.analogy: Jude is like a short, urgent memo sent to a team that warns them about people who are leading the company astray.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Ioudas, the same name as Judah, from Hebrew Yehudah.
common_mistakes: Confusing Jude with Judas, the disciple who betrayed Jesus.
Pronouncing Jude with a long u as JOO-duh rather than a single syllable JOOD.
nuance.biblical_note: Jude identifies himself in Jude 1:1 as a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, which likely means the brother of Jesus identified in Mark 6:3. The letter is short and urgent, warning the churches against people who twist grace into license. It quotes the Jewish book of 1 Enoch and warns of judgment on rebellious angels and ungodly people. Jude 1:3 urges believers to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.

senses.definition: The power, right, or authority to interpret and apply the law.
senses.example: legal jurisdiction

senses.definition: The power or right to exercise authority.
senses.example: outside the jurisdiction of

senses.definition: The power or right to perform some action as part of applying the law.
senses.example: Police officers have no jurisdiction in that district.

senses.definition: The authority of a sovereign power to govern or legislate.
The limits or territory within which authority may be exercised.
senses.example: The United Kingdom consists of three jurisdictions: England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
